title: Test design: Count in Range
summary: Count the values between two bounds. Most cases look alike; a few find the bugs.
spec:
`countInRange(nums, lo, hi)` returns how many values in `nums` are **at least `lo` and at most `hi`**: both bounds are included.

If `lo` is greater than `hi`, the range is empty and the answer is `0`. An empty array gives `0`.

variants.title: Leaves out values equal to hi
variants.defect: The comparison is v < hi, so a value exactly at the upper bound isn't counted.
variants.gap: Every value in your cases sits strictly inside or clearly outside the range. What happens to a value that equals one of the bounds exactly?

variants.title: Leaves out values equal to lo
variants.defect: The comparison is v > lo, so a value exactly at the lower bound isn't counted.
variants.gap: Try a value that equals lo exactly: is it inside the range or not, according to the specification?

variants.title: Never looks at the last value
variants.defect: The loop runs i < nums.length - 1, so the last value is never checked.
variants.gap: In your cases, is the last value in the array ever inside the range? Where in the array a value sits can matter as much as its size.

variants.title: Treats a reversed range as if it were the right way round
variants.defect: When lo > hi it swaps them and counts, but the specification says a reversed range is empty: the answer is 0.
variants.gap: The specification says what happens when lo is greater than hi. None of your cases asks that question.

review_status: Written for practice and machine-checked: the reference and every faulty version were compiled and run with a real JDK, and each version's defect was shown on a case.
